title: Electric Charge and the Field — Physics at a Distance

info.text: Electrostatics is the foundation everything electrical builds on: charge as a two-signed, quantized, conserved property of matter; the inverse-square force between charges; the electric field that replaces action at a distance; the potential landscape that stores energy per charge; and the conductor–insulator behavior that decides where charge can go. Sorting these terms reconstructs the ladder, one idea earning the next.

clusters.name: What charge is
clusters.fact: Charge is matter's two-signed bookkeeping property: it comes only in whole multiples of the elementary charge, and an isolated system's total never changes. An atom carrying extra or missing charge is an ion; net zero is neutral.

electric charge.text: Matter's two-signed physical property, measured in coulombs: what makes charges repel or attract and what every electrical quantity keeps track of.

ion.text: An atom or molecule with a net charge from gaining electrons (negative anion) or losing them (positive cation).

elementary charge.text: The quantum of charge, e ≈ 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ coulomb, the magnitude one electron or proton carries; all charge comes in integer multiples of it. Its size was measured by Millikan's oil-drop experiment.

conservation of charge.text: The total charge of an isolated system never changes: rubbing, ionizing, and current only move charge around, never create or destroy it.

electrically neutral.text: Net charge of zero — positive and negative charge exactly balanced. Neutral objects still respond to nearby charges by polarizing.

info.text: The bookkeeping layer: what charge is, that it is quantized and conserved, and the words for an object's net amount — ion on one side, neutral at zero.

clusters.name: The Coulomb force
clusters.fact: Two charges push or pull along the line between them with a force proportional to the product of their charges and to the inverse square of their separation — like repels like, opposites attract. Coulomb measured it with a torsion balance.

Coulomb's law.text: The law relating two point charges: force along the line between them, proportional to the product of the charges, inversely proportional to the square of the distance. Published by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785.

electrostatic force.text: The push or pull between stationary charges — also called the Coulomb force; repulsive between like signs, attractive between unlike.

inverse-square law.text: A force that weakens with the square of the distance: double the separation, one quarter the force. Gravity follows the same pattern, a resemblance the sources draw explicitly.

torsion balance.text: Coulomb's instrument: a bar suspended by a thin fiber whose twist measures the tiny repulsion between charged spheres.

info.text: The quantitative law of attraction and repulsion, the inverse-square shape it shares with gravity, and the instrument that first pinned it down.

clusters.name: The field idea
clusters.fact: A charge fills the space around it with an electric field: the force a vanishingly small test charge would feel, per unit of its charge. Fields from several charges add vectorially, and field lines trace the direction a positive charge would be pushed.

electric field.text: The force per unit charge at each point of space, in volts per meter: a property of space set by the charges that are there. Measured in V/m, equivalent to N/C.

field line.text: A drawn curve tangent to the field everywhere, pointing the way a positive charge would be pushed; introduced by Faraday as lines of force. Line density shows strength.

test charge.text: The idealized vanishingly small charge used to probe a field without disturbing it — the q in E = F/q.

superposition principle.text: Fields from several charges add as vectors: the net field at a point is the vector sum of what each source contributes alone.

info.text: The field reframes force-at-a-distance as a condition of space: defined per unit charge, probed with a test charge, drawn as field lines, combined by superposition.

clusters.name: Charge in matter
clusters.fact: Conductors hold electrons free to roam; insulators hold their charge fixed in place. Rubbing two materials together can transfer charge — the triboelectric effect — leaving an object with motionless net charge: static electricity.

conductor.text: A material — metal, saltwater, graphite — with charges free to move through it; excess charge spreads over its surface and drains to any contact. The word was coined by John Desaguliers after Stephen Gray's conduction experiments.

insulator.text: A material whose charges are bound in place — glass, rubber, plastic — so it can hold a separated or excess charge indefinitely. Desaguliers' name for Gray's non-conductors.

static electricity.text: The phenomenon of nonzero net charge at rest on a surface: the crackle of a sweater, the spark from a doorknob. 'Static' because the charge is not flowing.

triboelectric effect.text: Charge transfer between two materials pressed and separated — the ancient amber-on-wool observation that gives electricity its name (ēlektron, amber).

info.text: Where charge can and cannot move: the two material classes, how rubbing transfers charge, and why stuck-on charge stays stuck.

clusters.name: Polarization and induction
clusters.fact: A nearby charge redistributes charge in a neutral object without touching it: free electrons shift in a conductor, molecules stretch into tiny dipoles in an insulator. The near side ends up with opposite charge — which is why charged things attract uncharged ones.

electric polarization.text: The slight separation of positive and negative charge within an object — negative shifted toward a nearby positive charge, positive away — so the object stays neutral overall but acts charged locally.

electrostatic induction.text: Redistribution of charge in an object caused by a nearby charge, without contact. Ground the object meanwhile and it can be left with a real net charge of the opposite sign — charging by induction, found by Stephen Gray.

electric dipole.text: A pair of equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance — the stretched-molecule state an insulator's molecules take in a field.

info.text: The contactless response: how a nearby charge polarizes a neutral object and induces charge separation — the mechanism behind charged-attracts-neutral.

clusters.name: Potential and voltage
clusters.fact: Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge at a point, measured against a reference. Voltage is the difference in potential between two points, and equipotential surfaces connect points at the same potential.

electric potential.text: Potential energy per unit charge at a point, in volts (joules per coulomb), measured against a reference such as infinity; a positive charge slides from high potential to low, like a ball down a hill.

voltage.text: The difference in electric potential between two points — what '12 volts' across a battery terminal pair means; it is volts, not a stored substance.

equipotential.text: A surface of constant potential: no work is done moving a charge along it, and field lines meet it at right angles.

info.text: The energy view: potential as a value at each point, voltage as the difference between two points, equipotentials as level surfaces where no work is done.

bridges.fact: The two signs of charge are what Coulomb's law quantifies: the electric force between charges — push for like signs, pull for unlike — grows with the product of the charges and falls with the square of the distance.

info.text: The push or pull between stationary charges; also called the electrostatic or Coulomb force.

bridges.fact: The field is defined by dividing the electrostatic force on a test charge by that charge, E = F/q — so the field of a point charge follows straight from Coulomb's law, replacing action at a distance with a condition of space itself.

info.text: The defining division behind the field: force on a test charge divided by that charge.

bridges.fact: The field points down the potential hill (E = −∇φ): equipotential surfaces cut field lines at right angles, and moving a charge along one takes no work at all.

info.text: The rate at which potential changes with position — the slope of the potential hill the field follows.

bridges.fact: Whether an object keeps a net charge depends on its material: conduction lets charge flow away or spread through a conductor, while an insulator traps charge in place — which is exactly what makes static electricity stick around.

info.text: The movement of charge through a material — free in conductors, blocked in insulators.

bridges.fact: No contact is needed: the charged object's field polarizes a neutral one, pulling opposite charge to the near side — an induced attraction strong enough to lift paper or stick a rubbed balloon to the wall.

info.text: The field does the touching: polarization by a field creates opposite-sign charge on the near side, and unlike charges attract.

bridges.fact: Conductors and insulators answer a nearby charge in their own ways: conductors relocate free electrons across the whole object, while insulators only shift bound charge within each molecule — two limits of the same induction mechanism.

info.text: The two forms charge takes in matter: free charge that roams (conduction electrons) and bound charge fixed to atoms and molecules.

bridges.fact: Potential is defined by the work per charge of moving against the electric force; the potential of a point charge is Coulomb's law integrated over distance — the same interaction in energy language.

info.text: Pushing a charge against the electric force stores energy: work per unit charge is exactly what potential measures.

lenses.prompt: Which terms are statements about how much charge sits somewhere — the unit packet, a charged atom, or net zero?
lenses.explanation: These three pin down amounts: the indivisible packet (e), an atom carrying extra or missing charge, and perfect balance. Conservation of charge is a law about totals never changing, not an amount; electric charge is the property itself, not a specific quantity present.

reasons.elementary charge: The quantum e — the smallest amount that can sit anywhere.
reasons.ion: An atom whose proton–electron balance is off by whole units of e.

lenses.prompt: Coulomb's law is the full relation. Which two terms name its distance-falloff pattern and the apparatus that first measured it?
lenses.explanation: The pattern is the inverse-square law (double the distance, quarter the force); the instrument was Coulomb's torsion balance. Coulomb's law itself is the whole equation — charges and distance together — and the electrostatic force is the quantity it computes, not the pattern or the device.

reasons.inverse-square law: The falloff shape shared with Newtonian gravity.
reasons.torsion balance: The twisted-fiber apparatus of Coulomb's 1785 measurement.

lenses.prompt: Which terms belong to working with a field — probing it, drawing it, combining many sources?
lenses.explanation: The toolkit: a test charge probes without disturbing, field lines draw, superposition combines. The electric field itself is the thing being probed, drawn, and summed — not one of the ways of working with it.

reasons.test charge: The vanishingly small probe behind E = F/q.
reasons.field line: Faraday's picture of direction and strength.
reasons.superposition principle: The vector-addition rule for multiple source charges.

lenses.prompt: Which terms explain how an object becomes statically charged and why the charge stays put?
lenses.explanation: Rubbing transfers charge (triboelectric effect), the excess sits as motionless net charge (static electricity), and it stays put because an insulator's charges are bound — a conductor would drain it away. Conductor is the excluded opposite: it is what static charge could NOT sit on.

reasons.triboelectric effect: The rubbing that transfers electrons between materials.
reasons.static electricity: The motionless net charge that results.
reasons.insulator: Bound charges: the reason excess charge cannot leave.

lenses.prompt: A charged rod lifts neutral paper without touching it. Which terms name the steps of that trick?
lenses.explanation: First the rod's electric field reaches across the gap; then induction redistributes charge in the paper; polarization is the resulting separation — opposite charge nearer the rod — so the net attraction follows. The electric dipole is the shape the paper's molecules take, not a step in the mechanism, and the electrostatic force is the final attraction, not how it is achieved.

reasons.electric field: Reaches across the gap — no contact needed.
reasons.electrostatic induction: Charge redistributes in the neutral object.
reasons.electric polarization: Opposite charge ends up on the near side; unlike charges attract.

lenses.prompt: Potential has a value at every point. Which terms compare that value across locations rather than define it at one?
lenses.explanation: Voltage is the difference between two points; an equipotential joins points sharing the same value, so the difference across it is zero. Electric potential itself is the at-a-point definition — the quantity the other two compare.

reasons.voltage: Potential difference between two points — a battery's job to maintain.
reasons.equipotential: All points equal: zero difference, zero work moving along it.

entries.reason: Next rung of the ladder: the charges this board introduces at rest become the currents that do work — this board's conductors and potential carry straight over.
The board that closes the circle: moving charge — currents — turns out to be the source of all magnetism, and changing fields push back.

learningIntroduction.title: Physics at a distance
learningIntroduction.summary: Trace electrostatics from charge as a conserved property to the field, induction, and the potential landscape — the ladder every electrical idea stands on.

content.text:
Rub a balloon on your hair and it will stick to a wall. Nothing touched the wall. The explanation runs through the ideas this subject teaches, in a strict order: what charge is, how charges push and pull, how a charge fills space with a field, what charge does inside materials, and how the whole story can be retold in the language of energy.

Start with charge itself. It is not a substance or a fluid; it is a property that matter carries, in two signs that Benjamin Franklin named positive and negative. Two facts make charge easy to bookkeep. First, it is quantized: every bit of charge is a whole-number multiple of the elementary charge, the tiny amount one electron or proton carries. Rubbing does not create charge — it transfers electrons between surfaces, the triboelectric effect, discovered when the ancients rubbed amber and it attracted lint. Second, it is conserved: the total charge of an isolated system never changes. An object with extra charge is negatively charged, one with a deficit is positive, an atom that gained or lost electrons is an ion, and an object with exactly equal positive and negative charge is electrically neutral — net zero. A charged object's stuck-on excess is static electricity, and it stays put only on insulators, because a conductor would let it drain away.

How strongly do two charges interact? Coulomb's law answers with a force along the line between them, proportional to the product of the two charges and to the inverse square of the separation — the same inverse-square pattern gravity follows, which is why an inverse-square law is a family resemblance among forces. Coulomb confirmed it in 1785 with a torsion balance, measuring the twist of a suspended bar pushed by repulsion. Like signs repel, opposite signs attract: that asymmetry between the two signs is what the law quantifies.

Coulomb's law, though, describes a force reaching across empty space — action at a distance, which physicists found philosophically uncomfortable. The field idea replaces it. Each charge fills the space around it with an electric field, defined as the force per unit charge that a vanishingly small test charge would feel at each point. The field is a property of space itself: it exists whether or not another charge is around to feel it. Fields from several charges add vectorially — the superposition principle — and field lines draw the picture, their direction the way a positive charge would be pushed, their density the field's strength. Bring a charged object near a neutral one and its field does something remarkable: it polarizes the neutral object, shifting free electrons through a conductor or stretching each molecule into a tiny electric dipole in an insulator. The near side acquires opposite charge, so the two attract — no contact required. That is electrostatic induction, and it is why the balloon holds the wall.

Finally, the energy retelling. Force describes pushes; potential describes hills. The electric potential at a point is the potential energy per unit charge a small charge would have there, measured against a reference like infinity. A voltage — the word from the fact that potential is measured in volts — is the difference in potential between two points, the thing a battery maintains between its terminals. Equipotential surfaces connect points of equal potential, cutting field lines at right angles, and moving a charge along one takes no work. The field, it turns out, always points down the potential hill.

Charge, force, field, matter, potential: five rungs, one ladder. Every electrical device — wire, battery, motor, radio — stands on it.
